speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: A public consultation exercise on the draft bill was held from 12 May to 4 June this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) has evaluated the feedback received and, where relevant, incorporated them in the final Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: I will deal with each of these in turn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: First, we will extend customer accounting to prescribed supplies commonly used in GST fraud.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Currently, GST-registered businesses charge GST on taxable supplies when they sell to other businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Businesses which purchase such supplies consequently pay GST on those purchases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: They are allowed to offset the GST they pay for their purchases against the GST they collect on their sales and pay the net difference to the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Let us, say, we have a GST-registered business "A". "A" sells taxable supplies at a price inclusive of GST of $8 to another GST-registered business "B". "B" sells the goods to customers like you and I at a higher price because he needs to make a profit and charges us GST of $9.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: In this situation, "A" must pay to IRAS the $8 output tax which he collected from "B". "B", in turn, must pay IRAS the output tax of $9 which he collected from us, but he can offset that against the $8 input tax which he paid to "A".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: So, at the end of the day, "B" only needs to remit to IRAS the difference between his output GST, what he charges his customers, and his input GST, which is what he paid "A", and that net is $1.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: So, this means that at the end of the day, IRAS collects a total of $9 GST from the entire transaction: $8 from "A" and $1 from "B".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: However, IRAS has come across cases where "A" absconds with the GST collected from "B", and businesses like "B" further along the supply chain continue to claim the input tax.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: When that happens, IRAS is now short by the amount of tax which "A" has absconded with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: So, using the example above, if "A" absconds with the output tax, but "B" continues to offset his input tax, it means that, at the end of the day, IRAS only receives $1 instead of the $9 which should rightfully have been paid to it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The proposed amendments seek to avoid this scenario from happening by introducing customer accounting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Under customer accounting, GST-registered sellers like "A" will no longer charge GST on the sale of prescribed supplies to GST-registered business customers like "B".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Instead, the GST-registered business customers, that is, "B", will self-account to IRAS for the GST chargeable, as output tax and, at the same time, claim input tax on these purchases, which will exactly offset the output tax.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: This will deter fraud schemes, such as the scenario described earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Customer accounting will not apply to all goods and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: These goods are commonly used in GST fraud.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: We will monitor the situation and assess if there is a need to prescribe more goods or services, taking into consideration the impact on businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 2 to 4 of the Bill provide for the changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Second, we will amend the Act such that the Comptroller can require selected businesses to maintain an electronic inventory system with details of sales and purchases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The Comptroller can also require additional details, such as the model and serial number of the goods, to be provided in invoices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: These additional requirements will facilitate the identification of goods in the event of a GST audit and apply to selected businesses identified on a risk assessment basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: These businesses will be informed in writing of the requirements, and sufficient time will be given for implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 5 and 7 of the Bill provides for the changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Currently, a penalty of $200 is imposed for each completed month that the return remains outstanding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: A GST-registered business is not penalised even if it is late in filing its return after the filing due date, as long as it files within one month of the due date.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: This is unfair to businesses which respect the due date as the due date and file on time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: A $200 penalty imposed at the point of the GST filing due date will deter late filing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Clause 9 of the Bill provides for the change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: As digital tax notices for property tax, GST and income tax will be rolled out in phases, starting with property tax, I will elaborate on this change in my speech on the Property Tax (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The remaining legislative changes are intended to ease business compliance or clarify existing legislation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, as we strive towards our goal of a Smart Nation, with digitalisation as one of the keys to achieving this, we should encourage and empower businesses to make use of existing technologies for administrative procedures.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Prime Minister’s National Day Rally speech has sparked much interest and discussion about going cashless.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This reminds me that, years ago, we started our pursuit for a paperless society when consumers were encouraged to switch to receiving their bills in digital formats.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This was not only to support environmental conservation, but also to make retrieval of records and transactions much easier for both consumers and business entities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Today, numerous apps have been created for the convenience of checking bills and even paying them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If consumers can benefit from going paperless, certainly, so can businesses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Having tax notices in digital formats will make record keeping more secure and manageable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Meanwhile, businesses may still opt out of receiving their tax notices in digital formats if they prefer hardcopies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This offers flexibility for those who may require time to adapt to the technology.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Understandably, making physical copies an opt-out option is a move to push businesses towards the digital format.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I have reservations for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and microenterprises.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these firms hire administrative employees who wear several hats.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And some of these employees are elderly, or even foreigners, and they may not be tech-savvy or know enough English to manoeuvre the digital options or choose to opt out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With many other administrative matters to cope with, they may then overlook the matter of paying taxes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the companies that have been falling behind payment?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If they are mainly SMEs and microenterprises, this will become an undue burden for them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Aside from higher penalty, we should find out the reasons for the late payments and see what can be done to help companies improve on this aspect.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These companies may be facing financial challenges, for example.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Having worked with as well as interacted with employers and employees in many SMEs, it is quite apparent that they have to deal with many challenges in these rapidly changing times.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From the labour crunch to digitalisation to administrative matters, these companies are facing pressures from multiple angles and they are struggling to stay afloat, let alone make profit.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For all the schemes that are available, some companies continue to be left behind.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To create an inclusive and welcoming business environment, we really have to do more outreach and display more empathy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As a result, will some SMEs overlook the notices from IRAS and end up being fined?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Before taking away the grace period, can the authority adopt other means to help SMEs submit their tax returns on time?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Ultimately, the amendments are clearly designed for greater convenience of businesses with their long-term interest in mind.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that many of the affected businesses would eventually ease into the changes and, hence, Sir, I support the amendments.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, Sir, it is, indeed, commendable that the Government conducted public consultations prior to debating the Bill in this House and I welcome the Bill in its entirety.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud the consultative effort that went into proposing a well-calibrated amendment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I support the move towards electronic notifications as changes to the framework for such tax notifications to be digitalised allows for alignment towards the National Smart Nation goals and aspirations.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, it is imperative for us to recognise that not the whole of the society will be ready for a total transformation to digitalisation and, therefore, no one in the society should be left isolated and helpless.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As such, it is good that the options for physical copies are still made available, especially for those who face challenges with the digital medium or are unable to catch up with the changes and can still have the traditional form of notification.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For this, I would like to suggest a deeper engagement with the community and also with the unions so as to assist in communicating the opt-out plans for less tech-savvy residents to continue to receive hardcopy notifications.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This may minimise or prevent further administrative delays resulting from late tax returns should the less tech-savvy residents be unaware that the notices had been sent.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is there any mitigating plan if property prices were to rise as a result of this change?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be any form of transitional grants to help these companies to ready them for adoption of standards/technology to counter the impact of this change?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, Sir, in conclusion, notwithstanding this, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The move towards further digitalisation is also a laudable one, in line with our Smart Nation initiative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The changes are also great examples of how the Government should take the lead in going paperless for the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am in support of the "opt-out" system for the digital tax notices and the move towards electronic recording keeping.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe and hope that we will do the same for other Government services and functions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has raised, this can be a hefty sum for SMEs, particularly as companies may require time to get used to digital notices reminding them to file their taxes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More importantly, I would like to ask for the reasons behind this change, given that tax compliance in Singapore remains high.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These sweeping changes proposed by this Bill may cause disruptions to the majority of businesses, which are largely compliant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I understand that with the rise of e-commerce, some countries, such as South Korea, Japan and Australia, have amended legislation to collect GST on goods purchased online from foreign companies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most recently, in September 2017, Malaysia also announced plans to tax foreign digital service providers, such as online shopping sites.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we propose this round of amendments to the GST Act, I would like to ask if the Ministry is also considering making similar changes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that a tax on cross-border goods could represent a sizeable revenue stream for the Government.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Members of the public have been talking about this and imposing this tax may not sit well with consumers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, a tax on discretionary spending may be less painful than alternative measures to collect additional tax, such as a blanket increase in GST.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: IRAS has been operating efficiently with the cost of collecting taxes remaining at a steady low, and tax compliance in our country remains high.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe our tax regime will only be further strengthened through this variety of changes, and I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the issues raised for the proposed amendment concerning digital tax notices, as this runs across all three tax Bills, I hope the Members would not mind if I address this in the following Bill, that is, the Property Tax (Amendment) Bill, which actually sets it out in more detail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I believe these three Members are also speaking on that Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Louis Ng spoke on the difficulties that SMEs and microenterprises might face on the submission of the GST returns.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The change is part of our periodic review of the GST system to improve tax compliance and to be fair to businesses that respect the due date and file on time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: SMEs and microenterprises are unlikely to be adversely affected by this change for two reasons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, most SMEs are not liable for GST registration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For those who choose to volunteer for GST registration, we encourage them to be compliant with our tax rule.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Businesses which face financial difficulties can contact IRAS to discuss alternative payment arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng and Ms Thanaletchimi noted that the amendment to deter GST fraud might cause disruptions and increase business costs to the majority of businesses which are largely compliant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we received suggestions about it during our public consultations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We understand the disruption and increased compliance cost to businesses and have studied the practices in other countries before proposing this change.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The type of GST fraud that we seek to deter has been encountered in the European Union (EU).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In response, many EU countries have applied customer accounting, or what they call domestic reverse charge, to similar supplies of goods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will provide more time for businesses to adjust.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also raised the threshold for customer accounting to apply from $5,000 to $10,000.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What this means is that the supplier will continue to charge GST to GST-registered customers on sales of prescribed goods that are $10,000 and below, and customer accounting will only apply if these sales are above $10,000.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will reduce the compliance burden on retail businesses, including mobile phone retailers, to carry out checks on small purchases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Further, mobile phones sold with subscription plans will be excluded from customer accounting to reduce the impact on affected businesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS has also published an e-tax guide and will reach out to businesses trading in such goods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To help businesses with system changes, IRAS will work with standard accounting software vendors on upgrading their software to cater for customer accounting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Thanaletchimi also asked whether the change in the sale of Government land with existing buildings to be demolished would affect property prices and translate into higher cost for businesses and individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The change is a minor amendment to clarify existing policy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If a building on a land to be developed is demolished, the GST treatment on such sale should follow the same GST treatment of the vacant land rather than the approved use of the building.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There will be minimal impact to businesses and individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In cases where such sales of land would now attract GST, GST-registered developers can claim the GST paid from IRAS as input tax.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We note Mr Louis Ng's comments on GST and e-commerce.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Minister for Finance, in the Budget this year, mentioned that with increasing digital transactions and cross-border trade, some countries have taken steps to adjust the GST system to ensure a level playing field between their local businesses which are GST-registered and foreign-based ones which are not.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are studying how we can do likewise.
